name: DR Congo
summary: Remains travel in a sealed international-standard casket with a death certificate, embalming certificate and health documents, plus a permit for transporting the body issued by a DR Congo embassy or consulate. Requirements on arrival are not officially published, so confirm with the consulate and the receiving funeral home.
documents: Death certificate (legalised; French translation advisable)
Embalming certificate
Certificate that death was not due to a contagious disease (usual practice; confirm with the consulate)
Permit for corpse transportation from the DR Congo embassy or consulate
Copy of the deceased's passport; if no valid Congolese passport, the consulate issues a substitute document (tenant-lieu)
coffin: Not officially published for entry. In practice, a hermetically sealed (zinc- or metal-lined) casket in a wooden outer case is expected for international air transport. Confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Embalming is standard for international transport. The rules for entry are not officially published.
consular: The DR Congo Embassy in Washington lists a 'permit for corpse transportation': USD 100 if the deceased has a valid passport, USD 150 if a tenant-lieu travel document must be created. Payment is by money order. Other missions charge their own fees. DR Congo is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: Customs and health clearance procedures at Kinshasa N'djili are not officially published. The family or a local funeral home collects the casket. Mortuary standards vary, and cold storage is limited outside Kinshasa.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
private_jet_note: Use an airport with customs and health services (e.g. Kinshasa N'djili) and confirm clearance with the handling agent beforehand.
export: The local funeral home, working with an international funeral director, obtains a civil-registry death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate giving permission to transfer the body abroad. After a violent or sudden death, a certificate identifying the body from the judicial police and district prosecutor and an autopsy report are needed, and the attorney general may order an autopsy without family consent. If the death was ordinary, the body is usually released within a few days. Few local undertakers can quickly supply international caskets. Cremation is not available in the DRC.
export_points: Death certificate from the hospital doctor (can take several days)
Embalming certificate and transfer permit from the local authorities
Prosecutor or police involvement after a sudden or violent death can delay release
Few local undertakers stock international caskets

at_a_glance.arrival: Funeral home collects; rules not published

steps.what: Appoint a funeral director and gather the death certificate and passport of the deceased.
Embalming, plus a health or non-contagious disease certificate.
Apply to the DR Congo embassy or consulate for the corpse transportation permit.
Seal the casket, then book the flight to an airport with customs and health services.
Customs and health clearance, then the family or local funeral home collects the casket.

key_points: A consular corpse transportation permit is required
Rules for entry at the airport are not officially published
Cremation is not available in the DRC
Cold storage is limited outside Kinshasa
authority: DR Congo embassy or consulate in the country of death; DR Congo health and customs services on arrival

name: Eritrea
summary: Eritrean consulates process the repatriation of Eritrean nationals: certified death certificates, two non-contagious disease letters, a funeral home preparation letter and proof of Eritrean nationality. A steel casket, or a wooden casket with a sealed steel liner, inside a wooden outer box is required.
documents: Two certified copies of the death certificate
Non-contagious disease letter from a state, county or municipal health official
Non-contagious disease letter from the attending physician
Funeral home preparation letter (procedures, casket contents, consignee name, address and phone)
Copies of the deceased's Eritrean passport or ID card, plus foreign passport or residence permit
coffin: The consulates prefer a steel casket inside a wooden outer shipping container. A wooden casket is accepted with a steel screw-down liner for sealing and a wooden outer box.
embalming: Not specified by the consulates. The preparation letter must describe how the body was prepared, and embalming is the usual practice.
consular: The consulates (e.g. Washington and Frankfurt) require Eritrean nationality, shown by an Eritrean passport or national ID or other proof. Documents are submitted by email. Fees and processing time are not published. Eritrea is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: Not officially published. Plan collection at Asmara by the family or a local funeral service.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight. Eritrea has strict entry and permit controls; obtain all authorisations before departure.
private_jet_note: Exit requires an airport immigration police approval letter, and flight permissions in Eritrea can take time.
export: To take a body out of Eritrea you need a death certificate issued by the Zoba (regional) Administration, the hospital death certificate form or dead body certificate, the passport of the deceased, a police clearance letter, an airport immigration police approval letter and an embalming certificate. The Zoba Administration also provides an English translation of the death certificate.
export_points: Death certificate from the Zoba Administration, with English translation
Police clearance letter and airport immigration police approval letter
Embalming certificate required
Passport of the deceased

at_a_glance.coffin: Steel casket or steel liner, outer box
at_a_glance.arrival: Confirm with a local funeral service

name: Ethiopia
summary: An Ethiopian embassy or consulate issues a free permit for shipping the body. It requires the death certificate, a non-contagious disease letter, a burial permit, the passport of the deceased and a funeral home letter confirming embalming and a hermetically sealed casket.
documents: Death certificate (original and copy)
Funeral home letter confirming embalming and a hermetically sealed casket (original and copy)
Non-contagious disease letter from the local health authority (original and copy)
Burial permit (original and copy)
Copy of the deceased's passport; if not an Ethiopian passport holder, a letter from the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs permitting entry
coffin: A hermetically sealed casket is required, confirmed in the funeral home letter.
embalming: Required: the funeral home must confirm the body was embalmed or preserved by standard methods.
consular: The embassy reviews the file and issues a permit for shipping the body, free of charge. The Washington embassy says it issues the permit quickly once the file is complete, and emails it to be printed in colour. Applications are rejected without a passport showing Ethiopia as place of birth, or without the Ministry of Foreign Affairs letter for non-passport holders. Ethiopia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The embassy says the transport rules for human remains are set by Ethiopian Airlines. Arrival is at Addis Ababa Bole, where the family or a funeral home collects the casket.
private_aviation: The embassy defers to Ethiopian Airlines for the transport rules. For a private flight, confirm with the Bole handling agent and the Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority how remains are cleared. No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. A private aircraft carrying a casket must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services; have the local handling agent and receiving funeral home confirm in advance that the remains can be cleared from a private flight.
private_jet_note: Ethiopian Airlines sets the transport rules; confirm clearance at Bole for a private aircraft in advance.
export: For a death in Ethiopia, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues a letter permitting repatriation (sometimes called a No Objection letter). It is issued after it receives a Letter of Release from the deceased's embassy, the local death certificate and any autopsy report. Most airlines require an autopsy before repatriation. Local undertakers can supply international caskets. Formalities normally take a week or more.
export_points: Ministry of Foreign Affairs No Objection letter required
Letter of Release from the deceased's embassy
Autopsy usually required by airlines
Allow a week or more

embalming: Required: embalming by the standard method of the country of death.
consular: Ghana missions authenticate the file. The Washington embassy charges USD 50 and asks for documents in triplicate (original plus two copies). arrival: Not officially detailed. The family or a Ghanaian funeral home collects the casket at Accra Kotoka. Cremated remains need the death certificate, cremation certificate and a hermetically sealed urn.

An export licence is needed, which the funeral director obtains. For transfer to the UK, the body must be embalmed and placed in a zinc-lined coffin. A post-mortem is performed when the death is unknown, unnatural, sudden or violent.
